segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with the rainbow over his head; his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he held in his hand a little scroll that lay open. He set his right foot on the sea and his left on the land,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he cried out with a loud voice, as a lion roars. And when he cried out, the seven thunders spoke with their own voices.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Seal up what the seven thunders said, and do not write it down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and swore by the one who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, and the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it:

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: but in the days of the sound of the seventh angel, when he is about to blow his trumpet, the mystery of God will be accomplished, as he announced the good news to his own slaves the prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke with me again and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go, take the scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Take it and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I took the little scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it up, and in my mouth it was sweet as honey; but when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

notes.note: The Greek word usually means 'foot' but can take in the leg as well, and the comparison to pillars suggests legs here. The same word is rendered 'foot' in verse 2, where the angel plants one on the sea and one on the land. Older versions have 'feet' in both places; most recent ones have 'legs' here.

The word is a diminutive of the ordinary term for a scroll, which is what a 'book' was at this period. Verse 8 calls the same object simply 'the scroll', so the diminutive may carry little weight. Whether this scroll is related to the sealed scroll of chapter 5 is debated.

notes.phrase: raised his right hand to heaven
notes.note: Raising the hand toward heaven was the gesture of a solemn oath. The scene closely echoes Daniel 12:7, where an angelic figure raises his hands to heaven and swears by the one who lives forever about how long it will be until the end.

notes.phrase: There will be no more delay
notes.traditional: there should be time no longer
notes.note: The Greek says literally 'time will be no longer'. Older versions took this as the end of time itself. Almost all modern scholars and translations read it as 'no more time will pass', that is, no further delay, which fits the 'but' that follows and the echo of Daniel 12, where the question is how long until the end.

The Greek verb is a past tense ('was accomplished'), used here of a future event that is treated as certain. English needs a future to make sense of the sentence. The verb means to bring to completion or fulfilment.

The phrase is a stock Old Testament expression, and English Bibles traditionally say 'servants'. The Greek word was the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way; applied to the prophets it expresses total belonging to God and was a title of honour. Many scholars accept 'slave' as the more accurate rendering, though 'servant' remains the majority choice in translations.

notes.phrase: Take it and eat it up
notes.note: The scene reworks Ezekiel 2:8–3:3, where the prophet is given a scroll to eat and finds it sweet as honey in his mouth. Eating the scroll stands for taking in the message the prophet must then deliver. The bitterness that follows here is usually understood as the painful content of that message, though the text does not explain it.

The verb is plural, with no stated subject. It may be an indefinite plural meaning simply 'I was told', or it may refer to the heavenly voice and the angel together. Some manuscripts have the singular 'he says', which older versions followed.

The preposition can mean 'about', 'against' or 'in the presence of'. Most modern translations choose 'about'; older ones have 'before', and some scholars argue for 'against', since the prophecies that follow are largely of judgment.

The Greek word rendered 'nations' here is the same word translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In lists like this one in Revelation, the peoples of the whole world are in view, so 'nations' is used.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators divide between 'slave' and 'servant'; readers would be misled if it varied chapter to chapter.
The formula εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων and related phrases recur widely, and a choice between 'forever and ever' and a more literal 'ages of the ages' should be made once.
In the period it meant a secret now disclosed, not a puzzle; 'mystery' versus 'secret' needs one decision across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
The verb recurs across the New Testament and is variously rendered 'preach the gospel', 'announce good news', 'declare'; consistency matters.
Translations vary between 'book' and 'scroll' (including 'book of life'); the physical object was a scroll and the choice should be uniform, along with the diminutive βιβλαρίδιον.
